title: Mince Pies
subtitle: small festive pastry cases filled with spiced fruit mincemeat
excerpt: Homemade mince pies use a short, crumbly pastry that is far richer than the thin commercial version. The filling is shop-bought mincemeat -- reliable, perfectly spiced, and ready to use. Dust with icing sugar and eat warm.
sourceNotes: A British Christmas tradition. Mince pies were originally filled with meat; the modern version is purely fruit and spice.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze unbaked in the tin. Bake from frozen adding 5 minutes to the time.
recipe.batchNotes: Double the batch and freeze half for gifts or later use.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make the pastry up to 3 days ahead and refrigerate.

content.text: Rich shortcrust is better than standard shortcrust here -- the extra fat makes it more tender and easier to eat in one bite. Do not overfill the cases; a teaspoon and a half of mincemeat is correct. Too much and the lids will not seal.

items.prepNote: yolk for pastry, beaten white for sealing

content.text: Rub the butter into the flour until it resembles fine breadcrumbs. Add the sugar, egg yolk, and 2 tablespoons cold water. Bring together into a disc. Chill for 30 minutes.
Heat the oven to 190C. Roll the pastry to about 3mm thick. Cut out 24 rounds with a 7cm cutter for the bases and 24 slightly smaller rounds or stars for the lids.
Press the larger rounds into a greased patty tin. Place 1.5 teaspoons of mincemeat in each case. Do not overfill.
Brush the edges of the pastry cases with a little beaten egg white. Press the lids on top and press the edges to seal. Make a small cut or pinhole in the top of each.
Bake for 18 to 20 minutes until pale golden. Cool for 5 minutes in the tin, then turn out carefully. Dust with icing sugar while still warm.

items.cause: Not sealed properly, or overflowed mincemeat broke the seal.
items.fix: Press the edges firmly and do not overfill. A little egg white on the rim helps the seal hold.

items.symptom: Pastry breaks when lifting from tin
items.fix: Leave for 5 minutes in the tin before loosening. Use a small palette knife to lift them gently.

content.text: Mince pies are eaten from Advent through to Twelfth Night across Britain. The tradition is old enough that the original mincemeat contained actual minced meat alongside fruit and spice. The fruit-only version became standard in the 19th century. They are offered to guests, left out for Father Christmas, and eaten in vast quantities throughout December.
